chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: Meanwhile, Moscow was empty. There were still people in it — perhaps a fiftieth of its former population — but it was empty. It was empty the way a dying, queenless hive is empty.
In a queenless hive no life remains, though at first glance it may seem as alive as any other.

The bees circle a queenless hive in the hot midday sun as cheerfully as they circle living hives; from a distance it smells of honey like the rest, and bees fly in and out the same way. But one need only watch that hive to see there is no longer any life in it. The bees don't fly the same way; the smell and sound are different. When the beekeeper taps the wall of the sick hive, instead of the former instant, unanimous humming of tens of thousands of bees with their abdomens threateningly compressed — producing with the rapid beating of their wings a living, aerial sound — the only reply is a scattered buzzing from different corners of the empty hive. From the landing board, instead of the old fragrant scent of honey and venom and the warm gusts of crowded life, comes an odor of emptiness and decay mixed with honey. There are no longer sentinels sounding the alarm with raised abdomens, ready to die defending the hive. Gone is the steady, quiet sound of pulsing activity, like the sound of boiling water — replaced by the discordant noise of disorder. Long black robber bees, smeared with honey, fly timidly and furtively in and out. They don't sting but crawl away from danger. Once, only bees loaded with honey flew in and left empty; now they fly out loaded. The beekeeper opens the lower part and peers in. Instead of the glossy black bees — tamed by labor, clinging to one another's legs and drawing out wax with a ceaseless hum of work — that used to hang in long clusters down to the floor, drowsy, shriveled bees crawl separately in various directions along the floor and walls. Instead of a neatly sealed floor swept by the fanning of wings, there is a floor littered with bits of wax, excrement, dying bees barely moving their legs, and dead ones that haven't been cleared away.

The beekeeper opens the upper part and examines the top section. Instead of tightly packed rows of bees sealing every gap in the combs and keeping the brood warm, he sees the intricate structures of the combs, but no longer in their former state of cleanliness. Everything is neglected and foul. Black robber bees prowl swiftly and stealthily among the combs, while the short home bees — shriveled and listless, as if old — creep slowly about without trying to stop the robbers, having lost all purpose and sense of life. Drones, bumblebees, wasps, and butterflies bump clumsily against the hive walls. Here and there among cells containing dead brood and honey, an angry buzzing can sometimes be heard. Occasionally a pair of bees, by force of habit, laboriously drag away a dead bee or bumblebee without knowing why. In another corner, two old bees languidly fight, or clean themselves, or feed one another, without knowing whether they do it as friends or enemies. Elsewhere, a crowd of bees crushes and smothers some victim, and the enfeebled or killed bee drops slowly and lightly as a feather onto the heap of corpses. The keeper opens the center frames to examine the brood cells. Where once there were dark, close circles formed by thousands of bees sitting back to back, guarding the high mystery of generation, he now sees hundreds of dull, listless, sleepy shells of bees. They have nearly all died without knowing it, sitting in the sanctuary they once guarded — a sanctuary that no longer exists. They reek of decay and death. Only a few still stir, rise, and feebly fly to land on the enemy's hand, too drained of spirit to die stinging him; the rest are dead and fall as lightly as fish scales. The beekeeper closes the hive, marks it with chalk, and when he has time, tears out its contents and burns it clean.

In the same way Moscow was empty when Napoleon, weary, uneasy, and grim, paced up and down before the Kammer-Kollezhsky rampart, waiting for what he considered a necessary — if merely formal — observance of the proprieties: a delegation.
In various corners of Moscow a few people still moved about aimlessly, following their old habits, barely aware of what they were doing.
When Napoleon was informed, with due caution, that Moscow was empty, he looked angrily at his informant, turned away, and silently continued pacing.
"My carriage!" he said.
He took his seat beside the aide-de-camp on duty and drove into the outskirts. "Moscow deserted!" he said to himself. "What an incredible event!"
He didn't drive into the city but stopped at an inn in the Dorogomilov district.
The theatrical coup had not come off.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXI
paragraphs: The Russian troops passed through Moscow from two in the morning until two in the afternoon, carrying the wounded and the last departing residents with them.
The worst congestion occurred at the Stone, Moskva, and Yauza bridges.

While the troops, splitting into two streams around the Kremlin, crowded the Moskva and Stone bridges, a great many soldiers — taking advantage of the delay and gridlock — turned back from the bridges and slipped stealthily and silently past the Church of St. Basil, under the Borovitsky gate, and back up the hill to Red Square, where some instinct told them they could easily help themselves to things that weren't theirs. Crowds like those at a clearance sale filled every passage and alley of the Bazaar. But there were no dealers calling out with ingratiating affability, no hawkers, no usual motley crowd of female shoppers — only soldiers in uniforms and overcoats, though without muskets, entering the Bazaar empty-handed and silently making their way out through the passages with bundles. The shopkeepers and their assistants (of whom very few remained) moved about among the soldiers in bewilderment. They unlocked their shops and locked them again, and carried goods away themselves with the help of their assistants. On the square in front of the Bazaar, drummers beat the muster call. But the drumroll, instead of drawing looting soldiers toward it as it once would have, drove them farther away. Among the soldiers in the shops and passages, men in gray coats with shaved heads could be seen. Two officers — one with a scarf over his uniform mounted on a lean gray horse, the other in an overcoat and on foot — stood at the corner of Ilyinka Street, talking. A third officer galloped up.
"The general orders them all driven out immediately, without fail. This is outrageous! Half the men have scattered."
"Where are you going? Where?" he shouted at three infantrymen without muskets who, holding up the skirts of their overcoats, were slipping past into the Bazaar passage. "Stop, you rascals!"
"But how are you going to stop them?" another officer replied. "There's no rounding them up. The army needs to push on before the rest scatter — that's all!"
"How can we push on? They're stuck on the bridge, jammed solid. Shouldn't we throw a cordon around to keep the rest from running off?"
"Go in there and drive them out!" the senior officer shouted.

The officer in the scarf dismounted, called for a drummer, and went into the arcade. Some soldiers started running away in a group. A shopkeeper with red pimples on his cheeks near his nose, wearing a calm, patient, calculating expression on his plump face, hurried up to the officer, swinging his arms ostentatiously.

"Your honor!" he said. "Please be so kind as to protect us! We won't begrudge trifles — you're welcome to anything, we'd be delighted! Please! I'll fetch a piece of cloth right away for such a distinguished gentleman, or even two, with pleasure. Because we understand the situation — but this here is just plain robbery! If you please, sir, couldn't guards be posted, at least to let us close up shop?"
Several other shopkeepers crowded around the officer.

"Bah, what drivel!" said one of them — a thin, stern-looking man. "When your head's been cut off you don't weep for your hair! Take whatever you want!" And he waved his arm energetically and turned sideways to the officer.
"Easy for you to talk, Ivan Sidorych!" the first tradesman said angrily. "Please step inside, your honor!"

"Talk indeed!" the thin one retorted. "In my three shops I've got a hundred thousand rubles' worth of goods. Can they be saved once the army's gone? Well, people — 'against God's might our hands can't fight.'"
"Come inside, your honor!" the first tradesman repeated, bowing.
The officer stood there, perplexed, indecision on his face.
"It's none of my business!" he exclaimed, and strode quickly down one of the passages.
From one open shop came the sound of blows and cursing, and just as the officer reached it, a man in a gray coat with a shaved head was thrown violently out the door.

The man, doubled over, rushed past the tradesman and the officer. The officer grabbed at the soldiers who were in the shops, but at that moment terrible screams reached them from the huge crowd on the Moskva bridge, and the officer ran out to the square.
"What is it? What's happening?" he asked, but his fellow officer was already galloping past St. Basil's toward the source of the screams.

The officer mounted his horse and rode after him. When he reached the bridge he saw two unlimbered guns, infantry crossing, several overturned carts, and frightened, laughing faces among the troops. Beside the cannon stood a cart harnessed to two horses. Four greyhounds with collars pressed close to the wheels. The cart was piled high, and at the very top — beside a child's chair turned upside down — sat a peasant woman, shrieking piercingly. He was told by his fellow officers that the crowd's screams and the woman's shrieks were caused by General Ermolov, who had ridden up to the crowd and, learning that soldiers were looting the shops while civilians clogged the bridge, had ordered two guns unlimbered and made a show of firing at the bridge. The crowd, crushing one another, overturning carts, screaming and squeezing desperately, had cleared off the bridge, and the troops were now advancing.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXII
paragraphs: Meanwhile the city itself was deserted. There was hardly anyone in the streets. The gates and shops were all shut; only here and there near taverns could solitary shouts or drunken songs be heard. Nobody drove through the streets, and footsteps were rare. Povarskaya Street was perfectly still and empty. The huge courtyard of the Rostov house was littered with wisps of hay and horse manure, and not a soul was in sight. In the great drawing room of the house — left with everything in it — were two people: the yard porter Ignat and the page boy Mishka, Vasilich's grandson, who had stayed behind in Moscow with his grandfather. Mishka had opened the clavichord and was picking out a tune with one finger. The yard porter, arms akimbo, stood smiling with satisfaction before the large mirror.
"Isn't it great, Uncle Ignat?" said the boy, suddenly banging the keyboard with both hands.
"Well I never!" Ignat replied, amazed at the broadening grin on his face in the mirror.

"Shameless! Shameless!" came the voice of Mavra Kuzminichna, who had entered silently. "Look at him grinning, the fat mug! Is that what you're here for? Nothing's been cleaned up downstairs and Vasilich is worn out. Just you wait!"
Ignat stopped smiling, adjusted his belt, and left the room with meekly downcast eyes.
"Auntie, I was doing it gently," said the boy.
"I'll give you gently, you monkey!" cried Mavra Kuzminichna, raising her arm threateningly. "Go start the samovar for your grandfather."
Mavra Kuzminichna flicked the dust off the clavichord and closed it, and with a deep sigh left the drawing room, locking the main door behind her.
Going out into the yard, she paused to consider where to go next — to the servants' wing for tea with Vasilich, or to the storeroom to put away what still lay about.
She heard the sound of quick footsteps in the quiet street. Someone stopped at the gate and the latch rattled as they tried to open it. Mavra Kuzminichna went to the gate.
"Who do you want?"
"The count — Count Ilya Andreevich Rostov."
"And who are you?"
"An officer. I need to see him," came the reply in a pleasant, well-bred Russian voice.
Mavra Kuzminichna opened the gate, and an officer of about eighteen, with the round face of a Rostov, entered the yard.
"They've gone away, sir. Left yesterday at vespers," Mavra Kuzminichna said warmly.
The young officer, standing in the gateway as if undecided whether to enter, clicked his tongue.
"How annoying!" he muttered. "I should have come yesterday. What a shame."
Meanwhile, Mavra Kuzminichna was studying with attention and sympathy the familiar Rostov features in the young man's face, his tattered coat and worn-down boots.
"What did you want to see the count for?" she asked.
"Oh well, it can't be helped!" he said in a vexed tone, placing his hand on the gate as if to leave.
He paused again, undecided.

"You see," he said suddenly, "I'm a relative of the count's, and he's been very kind to me. As you can see" — he glanced with an amused, good-natured smile at his coat and boots — "my things are worn out and I have no money, so I was going to ask the count..."
Mavra Kuzminichna didn't let him finish.
"Just wait a moment, sir. One little moment," she said.
And as soon as the officer let go of the gate handle, she turned and — hurrying on her old legs — went through the back yard to the servants' quarters.

While Mavra Kuzminichna was running to her room, the officer walked about the yard, looking down at his worn-out boots with a faint smile. "What a shame I missed Uncle! What a nice old woman! Where has she run off to? And how do I find the shortest way to catch up with my regiment? It must be getting near the Rogozhsky gate by now," he thought. Just then Mavra Kuzminichna appeared from behind the corner of the house, looking frightened but resolute, carrying a rolled-up handkerchief. While still a few steps away, she unfolded it, pulled out a white twenty-five-ruble banknote, and hastily pressed it into his hand.
"If his excellency had been at home — as a relative, naturally, he would have... but as things are..."
Mavra Kuzminichna grew flustered and confused. The officer didn't refuse but took the money quietly and thanked her.
"If the count had been at home..." Mavra Kuzminichna went on apologetically. "Christ be with you, sir! May God keep you safe!" she said, bowing as she saw him out.
Shaking his head and smiling, as if amused at himself, the officer ran nearly at a trot through the empty streets toward the Yauza bridge to catch up with his regiment.
But Mavra Kuzminichna stood at the closed gate for some time, her eyes moist, pensively shaking her head, feeling an unexpected surge of motherly tenderness and pity for the unknown young officer.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: From an unfinished building on Varvarka Street — its ground floor a tavern — came drunken shouts and singing. On benches around the tables in a dirty little room sat about ten factory workers. Tipsy and sweating, with glazed eyes and wide-open mouths, they were all laboring to sing some song or other — singing discordantly, straining, with great effort, clearly not because they wanted to sing but to prove they were drunk and having a good time. One of them — a tall, fair-haired young man in a clean blue coat — stood over the others. His face, with its fine straight nose, would have been handsome if not for his thin, compressed, twitching lips and dull, gloomy, fixed eyes. Clearly possessed by some idea, he stood over the singers, solemnly and jerkily waving his white arm — its sleeve rolled up to the elbow — above their heads, trying to spread his dirty fingers in an unnatural way. The sleeve kept slipping down, and he carefully rolled it up again with his left hand, as if it were very important that this sinewy white arm be bare. In the middle of the song, cries were heard from the doorway and porch — fighting and blows. The tall young man waved his arm.
"Stop it!" he commanded. "There's a fight, boys!" And still rolling up his sleeve, he went out to the porch.

The factory workers followed him. These men, who under the tall fellow's leadership had been drinking at the tavern since morning, had brought the publican some skins from the factory and in return had been served drinks. Blacksmiths from a neighboring smithy, hearing the sounds of revelry and assuming the tavern had been broken into, tried to force their way in too, and a fight at the door had resulted.
The publican was wrestling with one of the smiths at the doorway, and when the workers came out, the smith wrenched free and fell face-down on the pavement.
Another smith tried to push through the doorway, pressing his chest against the publican.
The tall young man punched the smith in the face and shouted wildly: "They're attacking us, boys!"
At that moment the first smith got up and, scratching his bruised face to make it bleed, shouted in a tearful voice: "Police! Murder! They've killed a man, boys!"
"Oh dear God — a man beaten to death! Killed!" screamed a woman coming out of a gate nearby.
A crowd gathered around the bloodied smith.
"Haven't you robbed people enough — taking the shirts off their backs?" a voice addressed the publican. "What have you killed a man for, you thief?"
The tall young man, standing on the porch, turned his bleary eyes from the publican to the smith and back, as if deciding whom to fight next.
"Murderer!" he suddenly shouted at the publican. "Grab him, boys!"
"Ha! You'd like to grab me, would you?" the publican shouted, pushing away the men advancing on him, and snatching his cap from his head, he flung it to the ground.
As if this action held some mysterious, menacing significance, the workers surrounding the publican paused in indecision.
"I know the law perfectly well, friends! I'll take this to the police captain. You think I can't reach him? Robbery isn't allowed anymore!" the publican shouted, picking up his cap.
"Come along then! Come along then!" the publican and the tall young man repeated after each other, and they moved up the street together.
The bloodied smith walked alongside them. The factory workers and others followed, talking and shouting.

At the corner of Moroseyka Street, opposite a large house with closed shutters that bore a bootmaker's sign, stood a score of thin, worn-out, gloomy-faced cobblers in overalls and long, tattered coats.
"He should pay his workers properly," a thin workman with a furrowed brow and scraggly beard was saying.
"But he's sucked our blood and now thinks he's done with us. He's been stringing us along all week, and now that he's brought us to this pass, he's disappeared."
Seeing the crowd and the bloodied man, the cobbler fell silent, and with eager curiosity all the bootmakers joined the moving crowd.
"Where are all these people going?"
"To the police, of course!"
"I say, is it true that we've been defeated?" "What did you think? Look at what people are saying."
Questions and answers flew. The publican, taking advantage of the growing crowd, dropped back and returned to his tavern.

The tall young man, not noticing that his adversary had disappeared, waved his bare arm and went on talking without pause, drawing everyone's attention. It was around him that the crowd chiefly gathered, expecting him to answer the questions on everyone's mind.

"He has to keep order — keep the law — that's what the government is for. Am I right, good Christians?" said the tall young man with a barely perceptible smile. "He thinks there's no government! How can you get by without government? Otherwise there'd be plenty of people robbing us."

"Why talk nonsense?" voices in the crowd replied. "Will they just hand over Moscow like that? They told you that as a joke and you believed it! There are plenty of troops on the march! Let him in, indeed! That's what the government is for. You'd better listen to what people are saying," said some in the mob, pointing at the tall young man.
By the wall of China-Town, a smaller group had gathered around a man in a rough coat who held a paper in his hand.
"A decree! They're reading a decree!" voices cried, and the crowd rushed toward the reader.

The man in the rough coat was reading Rostopchin's broadsheet of August 31. When the crowd gathered around him he seemed flustered, but at the demand of the tall young man, who had pushed his way to the front, he began in a rather trembling voice to read the sheet from the beginning.

"Early tomorrow I shall go to his Serene Highness" — he read ("Sirin Highness," said the tall fellow with a triumphant smile and a frown) — "to consult with him, to act, and to help the army destroy these scoundrels. We too shall take part..." the reader continued, then paused. ("See?" the young man shouted victoriously. "He's going to sort the whole thing out for you!") "...in destroying them, and will send these visitors to the devil. I shall come back for dinner, and we'll get to work. We will deal with them, completely deal with and undo these scoundrels."

The last words were read into total silence. The tall fellow hung his head gloomily. It was clear that nobody understood the ending. In particular, the words "I shall come back for dinner" displeased both reader and audience. The crowd's mood had been pitched high, and this was too simple and unnecessarily plain — it was the sort of thing any of them might say, and therefore not what a decree from the highest authority should contain.
They all stood there, dejected and silent. The tall young man moved his lips and swayed from side to side.

"We should ask him... that's the man himself?" ... "Yes, ask him! Why not? He'll explain..." voices at the back of the crowd were suddenly heard saying, and everyone's attention turned to the police superintendent's carriage, which drove into the square escorted by two mounted dragoons.

The superintendent of police — who had gone that morning, on Rostopchin's orders, to burn the barges and had in connection with that errand acquired a large sum of money now sitting in his pocket — on seeing the crowd bearing down on him, told his driver to stop.
"What people are these?" he shouted at the men moving individually and timidly toward his carriage.
"What people are these?" he shouted again, getting no answer.

"Your honor," the shopkeeper in the rough coat replied, "your honor, in keeping with the proclamation of his highest excellency the count, they wish to serve without sparing their lives, and it is not any kind of riot — it is just as his highest excellency said..."
"The count has not left — he is here — and an order will be issued concerning you," said the superintendent. "Drive on!" he told his coachman.
The crowd stopped, pressing around those who had heard what the superintendent said, and watched the departing carriage.
The superintendent of police turned around at that moment with a frightened look, said something to his driver, and his horses picked up speed.

"It's a trick, boys! Take us to the man himself!" shouted the tall young man. "Don't let him go, boys! Make him answer! Hold him!" shouted various voices, and the crowd dashed in pursuit of the carriage.
Following the superintendent of police, talking loudly, the crowd moved in the direction of Lubyanka Street.
"So the gentry and merchants have gone and left us to die! Do they think we're dogs?" voices in the crowd were heard saying, more and more often.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: On the evening of September 1, after his meeting with Kutuzov, Count Rostopchin had returned to Moscow feeling humiliated and offended — because he hadn't been invited to the council of war, and because Kutuzov had paid no attention to his offer to help defend the city. He was also stunned by the new perspective revealed at camp, where the capital's peace of mind and patriotic fervor were treated as not merely secondary but entirely irrelevant. Hurt, offended, and bewildered, Rostopchin returned to Moscow. After supper he lay down on the sofa without undressing and was woken soon after midnight by a courier bringing a letter from Kutuzov. The letter requested the count to send police officers to guide troops through the city, as the army was retreating to the Ryazan road beyond Moscow. This was not news to Rostopchin. He had known Moscow would be abandoned not merely since his meeting with Kutuzov on Poklonny Hill the previous day, but ever since the Battle of Borodino — every general who came to Moscow after that battle unanimously declared it impossible to fight again, and since then government property had been removed every night and half the inhabitants had left with Rostopchin's own permission. Yet this information astonished and irritated the count, coming as a simple note with an order from Kutuzov, received in the middle of the night, breaking into his sleep.

When later, in his memoirs, Count Rostopchin explained his actions during this period, he repeatedly claimed to have been guided by two important aims: maintaining calm in Moscow and speeding the departure of its residents. If one accepts this dual aim, all of Rostopchin's actions appear beyond reproach. "Why were the holy relics, the weapons, ammunition, gunpowder, and grain supplies not removed? Why were thousands of inhabitants deceived into thinking Moscow wouldn't be surrendered — and thereby ruined?" "To preserve the city's calm," explains Count Rostopchin. "Why were bundles of useless papers from government offices, and Leppich's balloon and other items, removed?" "To leave the city empty," explains Count Rostopchin. One need only accept that public order is threatened, and any action can be justified.
All the horrors of the Reign of Terror were based on nothing but concern for public order.

On what, then, was Rostopchin's fear for Moscow's order based in 1812? What reason was there to expect an uprising? The residents were leaving and the retreating troops were filling the city. Why would the masses riot?

Neither in Moscow nor anywhere else in Russia did anything resembling an insurrection ever occur when the enemy entered a city. More than ten thousand people still remained in Moscow on September 1 and 2, and except for a mob in the governor's courtyard — assembled there at his own invitation — nothing happened. It is obvious that there would have been even less cause for unrest if, after the Battle of Borodino, when Moscow's surrender became certain or at least probable, Rostopchin — instead of stirring up the people by distributing weapons and broadsheets — had taken steps to remove the holy relics, the gunpowder, munitions, and money, and had plainly told the population that the city would be given up.

Rostopchin, though he had patriotic feelings, was an impulsive, hot-blooded man who had always moved in the highest administrative circles and had no understanding at all of the people he imagined he was guiding. Ever since the enemy entered Smolensk, he had been playing — in his own mind — the role of director of popular feeling in "the heart of Russia." Not only did he believe (as all administrators do) that he controlled the external actions of Moscow's residents, but he also thought he shaped their inner attitudes through his broadsheets and posters, written in a coarse style that the common people despise in their own kind and don't understand coming from those in authority. Rostopchin was so pleased with his fine role as leader of popular feeling, and had grown so accustomed to it, that the need to give it up and abandon Moscow without any heroic display caught him completely off guard. The ground slipped from under his feet, and he had no idea what to do. Though he knew it was coming, he didn't truly believe until the last moment that Moscow would be abandoned, and he made no preparations. The residents left against his wishes. If government offices were evacuated, it was only at the insistence of the officials, whom the count reluctantly obliged. He was absorbed in the role he had created for himself. As often happens with those gifted with vivid imaginations, though he had long known Moscow would be abandoned, he knew it only with his intellect — not in his heart — and did not mentally adapt to this new reality.

All his painstaking and energetic activity (whether it was useful or had any effect on the people is another question) had been aimed simply at arousing in the masses his own feeling of patriotic hatred for the French.

But when events assumed their true historical character — when expressing hatred for the French in words proved insufficient, when it wasn't even possible to express that hatred by fighting a battle, when self-confidence was of no use against the one question facing Moscow, when the entire population streamed out as one man, abandoning their property and thereby demonstrating through this negative act all the depth of their national feeling — then the role Rostopchin had chosen suddenly appeared senseless. He found himself suddenly ridiculous, weak, and alone, with no ground to stand on.

When, roused from sleep, he received that cold, peremptory note from Kutuzov, he felt all the more enraged because he knew he was partly to blame. Everything that had been specifically entrusted to him — the state property that should have been evacuated — was still in Moscow, and it was no longer possible to remove it all.

"Who is to blame? Who let things come to this?" he brooded. "Not me, of course. I had everything ready. I had Moscow firmly in hand. And this is what they've let it come to! Villains! Traitors!" he thought — without clearly identifying who the villains and traitors were, but feeling an urgent need to hate these people, whoever they were, who were responsible for the false and absurd position in which he found himself.
All that night Count Rostopchin issued orders, and people came to him from every part of Moscow. Those around him had never seen the count so grim and irritable.

"Your excellency, the Director of the Registrar's Department has sent for instructions... From the Consistory, from the Senate, from the University, from the Foundling Hospital, the Suffragan has sent... asking for orders... What are your instructions about the Fire Brigade? From the prison governor... from the superintendent of the lunatic asylum..." All night long such reports kept coming in.

To all these inquiries he gave short, angry replies indicating that his instructions were no longer needed, that the entire plan he had carefully prepared had been ruined by someone else, and that someone else would have to bear responsibility for everything that followed.

"Oh, tell that blockhead," he said in reply to the inquiry from the Registrar's Department, "that he should stay and guard his documents. Now why are you asking stupid questions about the Fire Brigade? They've got horses — let them go to Vladimir and not leave them to the French."
"Your excellency, the superintendent of the lunatic asylum has come. What are your orders?"
"My orders? Let them all go — that's all. And let the lunatics loose in the city. When madmen are commanding our armies, God obviously wants these other madmen to be free."
In reply to a question about the convicts in the prison, Count Rostopchin shouted angrily at the governor:
"Do you expect me to provide two battalions — which we don't have — as a convoy? Release them, and that's the end of it!"
"Your excellency, there are some political prisoners — Meshkov, Vereshchagin..."
"Vereshchagin! Hasn't he been hanged yet?" Rostopchin shouted. "Bring him to me!"
